body.text: Ask almost anyone who grew up in China in the second half of the 20th century about Xiǎo Yàn Zi, “Little Swallow,” and there is a good chance they will start singing. First published in 1956, the nursery rhyme opens as a gentle welcome to a swallow returning in spring. Its second verse, though, takes a distinctly industrial turn. The narrator tells the swallow that home is even “more beautiful” this year, “because we have built a big factory and installed new machines.” The narrator then invites the bird to stay for good. It is, in other words, a children’s song about industrial policy.

Seventy years since “Little Swallow” was written, China produces around 28 percent of the world’s manufacturing value added. Africa’s share of global manufacturing output, by contrast, has fallen from about 3 percent in the 1970s to less than 2 percent today, even as 10 to 12 million young Africans enter the workforce every year.

On November 20, as the continent marks Africa Industrialization Day, the question is a familiar one: when do Africa’s factories come? And next week, as African and Chinese senior officials gather in Brazzaville, the Republic of Congo, to prepare for the 10th edition of FOCAC, coming up next year also in Brazzaville, there is a more specific question too: has Chinese investment followed Africa’s industrial ambitions?

At Development Reimagined, we have spent the past year finding out. Our first report, “Beyond the Ore,” found $41.2 billion of Chinese mining and mineral investment across 15 African countries since FOCAC 9 in September 2024. Of that, $16.3 billion involved processing, refining, or manufacturing on the continent. That matters: turning bauxite into alumina can raise the indicative value of a tonne from about $32 to about $590.

In “Beyond the Ore,” we borrowed a Chinese saying to describe what makes this work: “the government sets the stage, and the private sector puts on the play.” Our new report, “Africa’s Factory Moment,” suggests that African governments have been busy building stages.

Between September 2024 and June 2026, African countries attracted at least $19 billion of Chinese manufacturing investment, across 113 projects in 19 countries and 13 industries. These range from cement and steel to textiles, vaccines, and electric vehicles. That is almost double the roughly $10 billion Chinese companies pledged to invest in Africa over three years at FOCAC 9, and it comes on top of the mining investment detailed in “Beyond the Ore.”

Some of the drivers lie in China, where firms from cement to EVs face excess capacity and fierce price competition, and abroad, where European duties and U.S. policy swings make producing in Africa increasingly sensible. But the stage matters too. Sixteen of the 113 projects were signed at forums held with African governments, or agreed with African public partners, from Egypt’s SCZone to Nigerian state governments and Zambia’s ZCCM-IH. And established industrial zones, such as TEDA Suez in Egypt and the Sino-Uganda Mbale Industrial Park, which now employs around 10,000 people, are drawing whole clusters of factories.

There is genuinely new ground here, too. Chinese companies are investing in clean energy manufacturing in Egypt, Kenya, Morocco, and South Africa. A Zambian-Chinese joint venture just broke ground on Zambia’s first cholera vaccine plant. In May 2026, a Chinese-owned factory in Uganda shipped its first 104 tonnes of canned pineapples to China. It was a small consignment, but a big signal about which way trade could flow. In many projects, African public partners are taking equity stakes of between 10 percent and 45 percent.

Still, there are limits. Chinese investment remains concentrated in Egypt, Uganda, and Kenya. Heavy machinery, logistics, and packaging have barely been touched, even though Africa imports about 51 times the value of the heavy machinery it exports. And factories alone do not guarantee that local suppliers, skills, or technology will follow. Those depend on the terms African governments negotiate, and on whether they negotiate together.
That brings us back to the upcoming talks in Brazzaville. Our report set out 24 recommendations ahead of FOCAC 10, including these three:
First, African governments should set the stage collectively, negotiating common terms on local content, equity, and skills.
Second, China should set a more ambitious investment target, weighted toward manufacturing rather than extraction, and make buying African-made goods an explicit objective.

Third, other international partners should stop treating Chinese investment in African factories as something to counter, and ask what they can add. Infrastructure for industrial zones and help meeting new carbon rules in export markets would be a good start.

At the end of “Little Swallow,” the swallow is asked to stay forever. That is the real test of Africa’s factory moment. The question is not whether investors arrive, but whether they stay, expand, buy from local suppliers, and train African engineers. If they do, in a few years’ time a child in Mbale, Ain Sokhna, or Ndola will be able to tell the returning swallows what Chinese children have sung about for 70 years: that home has become more beautiful, because of what was built there.
